Odfjell Drilling (ODL-NO): investment memo

Odfjell Drilling: a predictable 10% yield from five scarce rigs, but the earnings step-up is over and the share price rests on a weaker 2029

10 November 2026. Share price NOK 107.0 (USD 11.47) on 23 October 2026, the price used in the model. Market capitalisation USD 2.75 billion; 239.8 million shares. Money in USD millions unless stated. The forecasts and the thin, four-broker consensus are described in end note 1.

0.72 → 1.21 → ~1.0EPS (USD) in 2025, at the 2027 peak, and in 2029-30: the earnings step-up has already happened
10.5%dividend yield on a flat USD 1.20 a share from 2027: the case rests on cash distributions
3 in 4chance that 2027 EPS lands within 10% of 1.21; 2029, the year the share price rests on, is the least predictable year
11–11.5xmy central multiple of FY2029 EPS; the 13.73x guideline fair multiple is the bull case

#0 Summary of key insights, implications and conclusions

The practical conclusionAt today's price Odfjell Drilling is a fairly priced 10% income stream, not a skewed bet. The skew appears if the shares are bought after an overreaction to a rig-sized event, or if the company delivers one of two catalysts that are not in the forecasts: contracts that run into the 2030s, or a stated policy for returning surplus cash.
1
What you would own. Five harsh-environment rigs in the most protected corner of offshore drilling, fully booked through 2027 and run by the best operator in its basin. The earnings step-up is complete: EPS rises from 0.72 in 2025 to 1.21 in 2027 and then erodes to about 1.0. From here the investment case rests on cash distributions. The model has free cash flow of USD 5.7 a share over 2027 to 2030, half of today's share price, and a dividend of USD 1.20 a share, a 10.5% yield.
2
Predictability is the real asset. I put about three chances in four on 2027 EPS landing within 10% of 1.21, a degree of earnings predictability that few equities offer.
3
The positive skew Richard looks for is not in the earnings. Because the rig calendar is full, operating upside is capped at about 6% of EBITDA, while misses come in rig-sized steps of about 8% of a year's EBITDA for each lost rig-quarter. Consensus EPS is more likely to drift down than up over the next year, because the lead broker taxes 2027 profit at only 6% and the global minimum tax starts in 2027. The company gives no earnings guidance to beat. And the market has already embraced the positive story: every broker rates the shares Buy, and the multiple is at the top of its five-year range.
4
The shares are really priced on 2029 earnings, not 2027 earnings. The model values the shares at December 2027 as a multiple of FY2029 EPS. 2029 is the year in which five difficult events coincide (shown below). FY2029 EPS therefore has the widest range of outcomes of any forecast year (about 0.40 to 1.28 around 1.01), and the range leans down.
5
A positive skew could still come from two sources, neither of which is in the forecasts. The first is long contracts that extend visibility into the 2030s; the first test is Equinor's tender for Deepsea Atlantic. The second is a stated capital-returns policy once leverage reaches about 1.0 times, around end-2027. Both would lift the multiple rather than EPS.
6
The modelled return is a re-rating; the dependable return is the dividend. At the guideline fair multiple of 13.73 times, the model gives a total return of +36.2% to 31 December 2027. All of the share-price gain comes from the higher multiple: lower forward earnings subtract 12 points and dividends add 15.5. If the share price merely holds, the return is the dividend, about 10% a year. My central view is nearer the second outcome than the first.
7
How to turn this into a skewed bet. The shares have a record of overreacting to rig-sized operating events that leave the contracted cash flow untouched. Bought at today's high price, the case is a fairly priced income stream. Bought after such an overreaction, the case becomes a temporary cause for concern that clears, with a 13% dividend yield. The practical conclusion is to know the case in detail and wait for the price.

#1 Tailwinds in the operating environment; absence of headwinds

Evidence: the level of the market is strong. Rig supply is capped and demand is high and sticky.

Supply is capped

  • About 22 semi-submersible rigs can work on the Norwegian shelf, and 90% to 94% of them are working.
  • A newbuild rig needs a dayrate of about USD 720,000; leading-edge rates are USD 450,000 to 525,000.
  • Shipyards are full for about four years.
  • Reactivating a stacked rig costs USD 100 to 160 million and takes a year.

Demand is high and sticky

  • Demand comes from production maintenance (tie-backs, infill wells and exploration near existing infrastructure), supported by a 78% tax deduction.
  • Statistics Norway raised its estimate of 2026 oil and gas investment to NOK 266 billion.
  • Customers are booking earlier and for longer: within six months of the April 2026 incident on an Odfjell rig, Aker BP, Vår Energi and Equinor each committed to rigs ahead of need.

Evidence: the direction of the market is flat, and the dated headwinds cluster in 2028 to 2030. Leading-edge rates have not moved in two years, and nearly every recent fixture is at or below USD 500,000 a day.

  • Morgan Stanley forecasts Western European demand for floating rigs falling from 19 units in 2028 to 13 in 2030.
  • Transocean's harsh-environment fleet is 31% uncommitted in 2028 and 74% uncommitted in 2030.
  • Equinor targets a 30% lower cost per well, and Aker BP is past its peak investment year.
  • Norwegian offshore wages rise 4% to 5% a year while contract reset rates are flat.
  • The global minimum tax starts in 2027.
  • Brent is at USD 111, and the sector view weakens if Brent falls below USD 85.

Inference. Rig scarcity now buys contract duration, not higher prices. The operating environment sets a floor under 2027 earnings and gives no lift after 2027. The change in trend to watch for is a change of sign in 2029, from a market short of rigs to a market asking how many rigs it needs. I differ from the earlier research in one respect. The main threat to Odfjell is not new rigs entering the market, because the pool of available rigs is nearly empty: Deepsea Mira goes to Trinidad, Seadrill's two stacked units need USD 100 million each to return, and the COSL and Dolphin rigs are contracted to 2030 or 2031. The main threat is incumbents' rigs coming free as demand steps down.

So what. Full utilisation at current rates is safe to 2027, but nothing in the external environment adds growth. The share price will turn on whether operators sign rig-years for 2029 to 2031 during 2027.

Strongest counter-case. The demand step-down is a forecast, not a fact. Equinor plans about 250 wells to 2035 and six to eight tie-backs a year; 2.8 billion barrels in tight reservoirs were mapped in October; rig supply cannot grow; and Transocean Norge has been fixed at USD 517,000 to 558,000 a day for 2028. If rates step up, three of Odfjell's five rigs carry market-linked pricing in 2028 and would capture the increase.

Against the market. I agree with the market's narrative ("no newbuilds, so visibility pays") up to 2028. I differ on 2029 to 2030: the demand forecasts exist in sector research, but nobody has tied them to Odfjell's own calendar of contract resets.

What would change my view. Up: awards for 2029 to 2031 of three years or more at USD 480,000 a day or above; a broker-set 2028 rate for Deepsea Nordkapp above USD 480,000. Down: a Nordkapp rate below USD 440,000; shorter award terms; cuts to Aker BP's or Vår Energi's spending plans; Brent below USD 85.

Conclusion: the tailwinds are strong in level and flat in direction, strong enough to protect 2027 earnings but not to grow them, and the headwinds are dated for 2029.

Score: 53, set by the Rater. Supply is capped (about 22 Norwegian semis, 90-94% utilisation, newbuilds uneconomic at USD 450-525k against about 720k needed) and maintenance-led demand is sticky, so the environment protects full utilisation to 2027; but rates have been flat for two years, wages rise 4-5% against flat resets, the minimum tax starts in 2027 and dated forecasts cut Western European floater demand from 19 to 13 units over 2028-30, so it adds no organic growth and starts to take margin from 2028. A strong level with a flat-to-turning direction is only a mild net positive, a touch below the External change forces group's 55, below OEM's modest recovery and just above Kerry's neutral.

#2 Internally-driven corporate change; absence of problems

Evidence: the large changes are done, and what lies ahead is mechanical. Odfjell bought Deepsea Bergen for USD 480 million, about 4.8 times EBITDA; refinanced its debt to 2031 at a fixed 7.25%; and more than doubled its quarterly dividend. Ahead lie no rig survey until December 2028, falling net debt and a further dividend step.

Three small positives are live.

  • The External Fleet, the rigs Odfjell manages for other owners, is growing again: Hercules for Suncor from Q1 2027, Mira for Shell from April, and a new management contract for Beacon Pacific. The External Fleet earned a 20% margin in Q3 against the 16% in the model.
  • A managed rig could be bought on terms similar to Bergen's, which would add 15% to 20% to EPS.
  • Management has said it does not want leverage below about 1.0 times.

The problems are real but modest. In 2026 the fleet lost about 170 rig-days to a dropped blowout preventer, stoppages of the riser package and a sub-vendor's labour dispute that ran through Q3. The spare blowout preventer has been used. Purchases from the related party Odfjell Technology are up 17% in a year. The board has four members and no committees, and the Odfjell family holds 49.85% of the shares. The company has no growth engine, and the chief executive has not yet renewed contracts in a soft market.

Inference. Corporate change has moved from building earnings power to deciding what to do with the cash. That capital-allocation decision is the only internal force that can still surprise the market. The arithmetic is less generous than the lead broker's. On the model, leverage reaches about 1.0 times at end-2027, and free cash flow exceeds the dividend by only USD 73 million in 2028. The surplus cash available by end-2028 is therefore between nothing (if the board holds leverage at a floor of 1.0 times) and about USD 0.6 a share (at a floor of 1.2 times). On DNB Carnegie's higher cash-flow forecasts the surplus is about USD 1.0 a share. A special distribution is therefore an option worth 0% to 9% of the share price, not a base case.

So what. Expect a harvest: a rising dividend, falling debt and low capital spending for two years. Do not expect the company to manufacture growth.

Strongest counter-case. The surplus cash could go into a late-cycle rig purchase at a fuller price, or a prudent board could hold it for the 2029 surveys. Either outcome would disappoint income holders.

Against the market. The lead broker has leverage sliding to 0.6 times by 2028. I think that will not happen, because the cash will be paid out or spent before then. Cash paid out is a positive that the market narrative has not yet drawn.

What would change my view. Up: a stated framework for capital returns. Either way: the price paid for any rig. Down: a second operating incident before the spare equipment is replaced.

Conclusion: corporate change is positive but nearly complete, and the single remaining lever, capital allocation once leverage reaches about 1.0 times, is real but smaller on our numbers than the sell-side implies.

Score: 54, set by the Rater. The large moves (Bergen bought at about 4.8x EBITDA, debt fixed to 2031, dividend more than doubled) are done and in the numbers; what remains is a mechanical harvest (deleveraging adding about 5% to EPS to 2028, a growing External Fleet, an optional rig purchase or special worth 0-9% of the price), net of about 170 rig-days lost in 2026, the spare BOP used, rising related-party purchases and thin governance. Gently positive but with no earnings lever and no rise in ambition, in line with Richard's CVS 55 reasoning and just under the group's 57, level with Shell's incremental self-help and above Hexatronic.

#3 Industry structure, competitive advantage, financial profile, management

Evidence.

  • Value chain. The driller keeps the margin: drillers earn an EBITDA margin of about 50%, against 5% to 8% at shipyards and 12% to 20% at equipment makers. Norway's regulator is the barrier to entry. Against that, three operators buy almost all the rig-days on the shelf and price much of them through independent brokers.
  • Competitive advantage. Odfjell's advantage is reliability. Its ten-year utilisation is 97%, against 85% to 92% for typical competitors, and its rig surveys have cost zero to 21 days off hire, against 62 to 70 days at Dolphin Drilling and SFL. Odfjell is paid for reliability in days worked, bonuses and early renewals, not in a higher base dayrate. The chief executive calls himself "a sucker for backlog".
  • Financial profile. The EBITDA margin is in the low 50s, against 31% to 40% at the large drillers; the post-tax return on capital is about 15%; the return on equity is about 20%; and free cash flow is about 1.4 times net income to 2028. These are cyclical highs, and there is nowhere to reinvest: the payout is about 100% of earnings.
  • Management. Management is operations-led and plain-speaking, and does what it says. Its ambition is deliberately modest (it calls the company "boring"). It has never bought back a share, even when the shares traded at 3 to 4 times EBITDA. Executives own very little stock.

Inference. Odfjell is a treadmill run exceptionally well, not a flywheel. Its advantage protects days worked and the odds of renewal, but the advantage does not compound and does not set prices. Against Richard's test of a dynamic team with stretching goals, the team is credible and disciplined but not stretching.

So what. Trust the days worked. Do not model a price premium, market-share gains or organic growth. The business deserves the multiple of a long but finite annuity.

Strongest counter-case. With supply frozen and the regulator's gate in place, the annuity may be renewable for a decade: Vår Energi holds options on Bergen to 2035, and Equinor holds options on Atlantic past 2030. Duration, not growth, could be what the market is underpaying for.

Against the market. I agree that Odfjell is the best operator. I differ on what "76% of 2027 to 2029 revenue covered" means: the cover is for days, not for price. As the table below shows, three of the five rigs take the market price in 2028.

What would change my view. Up: a tender won at a visible price premium; a share buyback. Down: evidence that Transocean's lead in drilling automation decides contract awards.

Conclusion: a favourable industry structure and a genuine operating edge produce an above-average financial profile, but the business has no pricing power of its own, no runway for reinvestment and a management that will not stretch.

Score: 58, set by the Rater. A supply-capped, regulator-gated corner where the driller keeps the margin and Odfjell is the reliability leader (97% ten-year utilisation, near-zero survey downtime), but three buyers price much of the work through brokers, the moat protects days not price, there is no reinvestment runway and management is disciplined rather than stretching. The financial profile (EBITDA margin 50%, p88; reported ROIC 7.8%, p56; about 15% post-tax on the memo, a cyclical high) is strong today but the industry's 2014-16 collapse and covenant waiver mean low through-cycle predictability; coherent with the groups (63, 50, 63, 61), so below Helios Towers' compounding unit economics and above Vodafone.

#4 Conservatism of guidance; managing the sell-side; record of delivery

Evidence: there is no earnings guidance, only statements about what the company controls. Odfjell gives no revenue, EBITDA or EPS guidance. What it does state: the fleet is booked to at least end-2027; the fleet's average dayrate is about USD 475,000 to 480,000 in 2027 and 2028; capital spending is about 100 in 2026 and 65 in 2027; leverage stays below 2.0 times; "indicated tax levels" rise with the minimum tax from 2027, with cash payments from 2029; and the dividend is "progressive".

The record of delivery on what the company controls is strong. Against brokers' forecasts, though, it beat twice in 2026 and then missed in Q3 without warning.

Inference. Management is an honest tracker, not a sandbagger, so there is no cushion to release. Nor does management steer the sell-side. On two lines the most-read broker is less conservative than the company itself: it models a 6% tax rate and 2027 capital spending of 40, against the company's own indications of a rising tax rate and spending of 65. Nobody corrects the broker. Over the next 18 months I expect six of the eight stated items to be met or improved, and two to move against shareholders: the tax level (about 80% likely to be quantified by the Q1 2027 report) and the survey budget for 2028 to 2030 (about 65% likely to be set above 50 a rig).

So what. The pattern Richard prizes (guide low, beat, raise) cannot happen at Odfjell. Good news arrives as contract and dividend announcements that the market already expects; bad news arrives as an operating report that nobody was warned about.

Strongest counter-case. The dividend is the real guidance, and it is conservative: the board raised it in a quarter that missed, and the 2027 dividend takes only 69% of 2027 free cash flow. The board has room to surprise.

Against the market. Some commentary calls Odfjell's guidance "structurally conservative" on the strength of two quarterly beats. I disagree, because those were beats of brokers' forecasts, not of company guidance.

What would change my view. Up: a capital-returns framework with numbers; a minimum-tax estimate at or below 12%.

Conclusion: delivery of what the company controls is excellent, but there is no conservative guidance to beat and no effort to keep the sell-side's expectations low, so this criterion is met only on track record.

Score: 58, set by the Rater. No earnings guidance, but the company guides on what it controls (fleet dayrate, capex, leverage, dividend) and delivers it: Atlantic back in 106 days against three to four months guided, every 2023-25 survey done, EBITDA up every year since 2022, broker beats in Q1 and Q2 2026; against that Q3 missed without warning, the survey budget crept from about 40 to 50 a rig, 2026 lost about 170 rig-days, and management leaves the lead broker's too-light tax and capex uncorrected, so there is no conservatism to release. Above 50 as a controllables-beater per the levels, coherent with the Guidance (56) and Sell-side (48) groups, just below Renew and above Entra.

#5 Pricing power, operating and financial leverage, cost scope, feedback loops

Evidence: the operating gearing is high and works both ways. Each rig earns about USD 590,000 per working day against a cost of about USD 238,000 per calendar day, almost all of it fixed, so EPS moves at least twice as fast as revenue, up or down.

  • Pricing power: Odfjell is a price-taker when contracts reset, and is protected on price (by escalation clauses and Norwegian-krone cost elements) while contracts run. Price adds about 1% a year to revenue against cost inflation of about 3%, so the EBITDA margin gives up 1 to 1.5 points a year from 2028.
  • Financial leverage: falling debt adds about 5% to EPS between 2026 and 2028, and then the benefit stops.
  • Cost reduction: there is no cost programme. The only cost lever is stacking a rig.
  • Feedback loops: the reinforcing loops (rig scarcity brings earlier commitments; reliability brings renewals) passed a hard test in 2026 and now hold the line. The balancing loops (faster drilling, the end of the wave of projects from Norway's temporary tax package, and wages rising against flat reset rates) act on 2028 to 2030.

Inference. The machine that turns revenue growth into outsized profit growth is intact, but with a full calendar and flat rates there is no revenue growth to feed it. From 2028 the same gearing works against the shareholder. One mitigating point is missing from the forecasts. About a fifth of Own Fleet revenue is not base dayrate (bonuses, currency elements and reimbursables), and reimbursable costs are passed through to customers at no margin. If a third of the cost base is passed through in this way, the model overstates the margin erosion by about 4 of EBITDA a year, or 10 to 12 by 2030.

So what. The only ways to re-engage the operating leverage are a sixth rig (about 100 of EBITDA) or an upcycle in rates (a 10% higher rate on a reset rig adds 16 to 17 of EBITDA per rig-year).

Strongest counter-case. The escalation clauses may recover more cost inflation than assumed, because their caps and floors are undisclosed, and reported cost per rig rose only "marginally" in 2025.

Against the market. The lead broker holds 2028 EBITDA at 591, against our 567. I think the market has not priced 3% cost inflation meeting flat reset rates.

What would change my view. Up: disclosed escalation terms that recover more cost inflation than assumed; contract resets above USD 500,000 a day.

Conclusion: operating leverage is high and proven, but it has nothing left to gear on the upside and becomes a slow drag from 2028, with no pricing power or cost programme to offset it.

Score: 63, set by the Rater. Structurally the operating gearing is large and proven both ways: costs of about USD 238k per rig-day are almost all fixed against revenue of about 590k per working day, incremental EBITDA margins were 84% and 71% on the way up, and EBITDA fell from 272 to 78 in 2014-15. But Odfjell is a price-taker at resets with price (+1%) below cost inflation (+3%), has no cost-out lever beyond stacking a rig, and financial leverage adds about 5% to EPS then stops, so it sits below the 75 level of pure proven operating leverage and close to the Economic strength group's 63.

Inference. Only one more year of double-digit EPS growth remains, 2027, and it comes from volume (the recovery of the rig-days lost in 2026) plus lower interest costs. After 2027 the forecasts decline: 2030 EPS is 16% below 2027 EPS. Compared with the last four years (revenue up about 11% a year, margin up 5 to 10 points), the next four years have higher levels of revenue and earnings but lower growth and lower margins. Odfjell has no way to grow faster than in the past without buying a rig.

I change no forecast input. I considered four refinements to the model. Two offset each other, two have no input line in the model, and none moves EPS by more than 1% (Appendix A).

Against consensus: we have no differentiated view on 2027 operations. Our 2027 EBITDA is 4.5% above the consensus median only because two of the four brokers have not updated their forecasts since the summer; it equals Fearnley's (610) and sits just below DNB Carnegie's (619). Our 2027 EPS equals the median by coincidence: our higher EBITDA is offset by our 14% tax rate, against about 10% in consensus.

Strongest counter-case. Deepsea Atlantic works continuously for Equinor at about USD 500,000 a day, contract resets come 3% higher and the tax rate stays near 10%. In that case 2028 EBITDA is about 630 and 2028 EPS about 1.32, instead of 1.09.

What would change my view. The dated outcomes of the five judgements in #9: Atlantic's 2028 work, the tax rate, the reset prices into 2029, and days worked.

Conclusion: the forecasts show a high, well-contracted plateau with one last year of 13% EPS growth and a gentle decline thereafter, in line with consensus on EPS and with no route to growth above the past.

Score: 21, set by the Rater. The reported measure is falling, so F; stripping the 2026 insurance gain (about USD 0.12) would give about +1.7%, but 2026 also lost about 90 excess rig-days worth more than that, so the honest base is no lower and the decline from the 2027 peak (1.21 to 1.02, -16%, consensus next-year EPS growth p3) is real. Placed at the top of the band because earnings stay well above 2025's 0.72, the growth that exists is organic and the margin holds near 49%, close to the past rather than collapsing.

#7 Scope for upgrades to guidance, estimates and narrative over 6 to 12 months

Evidence and judgement: the likely revision to each item, in date order, with my probabilities.

Inference. The stream of upgrades is switching from earnings to cash returns, and it is thinning. The remaining earnings upgrades are small and operational. The one sizeable revision still to come, the tax charge on 2027 EPS, is negative and has a date. The net breadth of revisions (analysts raising less analysts cutting), positive today, should be flat to negative by mid-2027. The arrival of 2029 in consensus matters for an income stock even if nothing goes wrong, because 2029 is the first published year in which free cash flow does not clearly exceed the dividend.

Sequence: the order of events flatters the near term. The next six months bring mostly small confirmations: the Nordkapp broker rate in December, Q4 results and the dividend in February, and possibly a contract for Atlantic. Months 6 to 18 bring the tax number, the first 2029 estimates and the survey budget.

So what. There is no upgrade cycle for the forecasts to feed. The narrative can still improve, but only through contract duration (for example, "booked through 2029") or capital returns (a stated framework), not through higher numbers.

Strongest counter-case. The minimum tax bites less than feared, because the exclusion for tangible assets works or the UK parent's losses shelter the profit. The tax rate lands near 10%, and EPS estimates hold while EBITDA estimates drift up.

Against the market. I am in line with consensus on EBITDA and about 15% below the lead broker on EPS, almost all of the gap being tax and financial cost. The shares also trade on about the same 6 times EV/EBITDA at which that broker cut its rating to Hold in February, calling the stock "catalyst light". A valuation downgrade is a realistic event if the share price rises another 10% without higher estimates.

What would change my view. Up: a tax estimate at or below 10%; an Atlantic award at USD 500,000 a day or more for three years.

Conclusion: upgrades over the next 6 to 12 months are likely to be small on EBITDA, slightly negative on EPS and confined to the dividend, so the scope for positive surprise is limited and narrowing.

Score: 35, set by the Rater. There is no earnings guidance to raise and the dividend step to USD 0.30 is already expected; FY2026 EPS is near certain to slip 1-3% after the Q3 miss, FY2027 EPS is likelier down than up (45% down over 2% once the minimum tax is modelled, 20% up), EBITDA gains are small catch-ups, and the first 2029 estimates show free cash flow about a quarter below 2028, against revenue growth of about 7% falling to negative. With a unanimous-Buy narrative that can only hold or worsen (a valuation downgrade is plausible) the scope leans mildly negative, coherent with the fourth set's 40, below IMCD and above TT Electronics.

#8 Current momentum: guidance, estimates, narrative, price, peers

Evidence: momentum is strong on every measure the dashboard pins.

The dashboard's pinned letters, snapshot 24 October 2026.

  • Price: the share price is up 55.7% in twelve months and stands 16.3% above a 200-day moving average that has risen in each of the last twelve months; its relative strength is in the 89th percentile of the universe.
  • Estimates: FY2027 consensus EPS is up 1%, 4%, 6% and 24% over one, three, six and twelve months. Over three months, however, consensus EBITDA is unchanged and consensus sales are down 1%. The recent EPS upgrades therefore came from the lines below EBITDA, which are the lines that reverse when brokers model the minimum tax.
  • Ratings: 100% of brokers rate the shares Buy, up 50 points in six months, and the mean target price is only about 6% above the share price.
  • Guidance: there is no earnings guidance to upgrade; the dividend was raised in November.
  • Latest data: the Q3 report on 3 November was the first miss of the year. The Phases data of 9 November shows a forward multiple of 9.2 times, against 10.0 times on 23 October, which suggests the share price has eased since the model's price date (end note 6).

Peers are weak and mixed. The sector basket fell 8.5% over six months while Odfjell rose 9.6%. DNB Carnegie says consensus must fall 15% to 24% for Transocean, Noble and Seadrill.

Inference. Momentum is strong, but it is the stock's own, it is late, and its quality is deteriorating: the upgrades have no operating content, the ratings cannot improve further, and the sector does not confirm the move. The share of Odfjell's daily price moves explained by its sector has risen from 5% to 8% in the summer to 20% now, so more of the next move will come from the sector.

So what. Momentum supports holding the shares. It does not support paying up, and it gives little cushion: a consensus in which every broker already rates the shares Buy cannot absorb a disappointment by upgrading.

Strongest counter-case. Relative strength inside a weak group tends to persist. Odfjell is where sector money hides, and flat estimates here are the best revisions in drilling.

Against the market. I agree that Odfjell is the momentum leader in its sector. I differ on how long that leadership will last.

What would change my view. Up: EBITDA revisions turning positive again. Down: the revision score falling to zero, or the share price falling below its 200-day average.

Conclusion: momentum is good today on price, estimates and ratings, but it is narrow, late-stage and unsupported by peers.

Score: 90, set by the Rater. Both measures in the top fifth with no part clearly negative gives A: FY2027 EPS up 1/4/6% over one, three and six months (3-month revision 8%, p87), 100% Buy (p95), price +55.7% over twelve months and 16% above a rising 200-day average; peers are weak but cannot pull the letter down on their own. Placed at the floor because the quality is thinning: EBITDA flat and sales down 1% over three months, the Q3 miss on 3 November, no guidance line to raise, and the price easing since 23 October.

#9 Riskiness and simplicity of the forecasts

Simplicity: the case is as simple as an equity gets. It consists of five rigs, days worked, a dayrate and a fixed cost, and it can be followed with about ten public observations.

Five judgements move the value most. In four of them a miss costs more than a beat adds.

  1. Days worked in 2027 (base: 95.5% utilisation). The asymmetry is two to one against the shareholder. One 100-day event takes utilisation to 91.5%. Four points of 1,825 rig-days is 73 days, and at USD 590,000 a day that is 43 of revenue. Costs do not fall, so EBITDA is about 40 lower (610 to 570); after 14% tax, net income is 34 lower, and EPS falls by 0.14 to 1.07 (-12%). Free cash flow falls to about 383, still 1.3 times the dividend of 288. A clean year at 97.5% utilisation adds about 20 of EBITDA and 0.07 of EPS.
  2. The tax rate from 2027 (base: 14%; range about 9% to 17%). Each point of tax rate is worth USD 0.014 of EPS. One point is 1% of pre-tax profit of 337.5, so 3.4 of net income. At a 10% rate EPS is 1.27; at 17% it is 1.17. The 17% case is my own scenario. Roughly 70% of profit sits in the Maltese rig-owning companies, taxed at about 5%. If the minimum tax's exclusion for tangible assets is denied, a 10-point top-up on about 236 of profit costs about 24; added to today's charge of about 34, the total is 58, or 17%. At a 14% rate the lead broker's 2027 EPS of 1.42 becomes about 1.30 (-8%). Cash is unaffected until 2029, and then pays about 10 to 20 a year more tax.
  3. Deepsea Atlantic's work in 2028 (base: about USD 470,000 a day with a probability-weighted 60-day gap). A long gap costs twice what continuous work adds. Continuous work near USD 500,000 adds about 30 of EBITDA, 26 after tax, so EPS rises by 0.11 to 1.20. A six-month gap takes off about 60 of EBITDA, 52 after tax, so EPS falls by 0.22 to 0.87; free cash flow falls to about 310, still above the dividend. A smaller open point is the rate on Atlantic's exercised option wells. One reading puts it at USD 413,000, which would take about 12 off 2027 EBITDA and 0.04 off EPS. I think that reading is unlikely. Given the other four rigs' rates (table in #3), the chief executive's fleet average of USD 475,000 to 480,000 needs Atlantic at about USD 500,000; at USD 413,000 the fleet average would be about USD 458,000.
  4. Reset prices into 2029 (base: flat in nominal terms at about USD 470,000). A 10% fall takes 20% off 2029 EPS and leaves the dividend uncovered. If resets come 10% lower, 2.75 rig-years reset by 2029, about 930 working days at USD 47,000 a day less, which is 44 of revenue; Stavanger's indexed rate following the market below its ceiling takes another 10 to 15. EBITDA is about 57 lower (552 to 495); after 14.5% tax, net income is 49 lower, and EPS falls by 0.20 to 0.81 (-20%). Free cash flow falls to about 233 against a dividend of 288, so holding the dividend becomes a choice funded by about 0.1 turns of extra leverage a year. Resets 5% higher add about 22 of EBITDA and 0.08 of EPS.
  5. The dividend yield the market asks for, which the board can influence. Each point of yield is worth about one turn of the multiple. On a USD 1.20 dividend, a 10.5% yield is today's USD 11.47 a share; a 9% yield is USD 13.33 (+16%); 8.7% is the guideline value; 12% is USD 10.00 (-13%); and 13%, where the shares stood in May 2026, is USD 9.23 (-20%). Each point of yield is roughly 9% to 10% of the share price.

Character of the risks: sudden operating events, slow market changes, sentiment shocks, and a cluster in 2029.

Sudden and unflagged: operating events. The base rate since 2025 is about one material event a year across five rigs. The group carries no loss-of-hire insurance.
Slow and trackable: market risk. Fixtures are made 12 to 24 months ahead and broker-set rates follow them, so a change in the market in 2027 reaches revenue in 2028 at the earliest.
Sudden and unrelated to fundamentals: sentiment. In April and May 2026 the shares lost NOK 17 on an incident the lead broker valued at NOK 3, and recovered in about three months.
Clustered: 2029, when three contract resets, two heavy surveys, the first cash minimum tax and the end of deleveraging coincide.
−86%offshore drilling equities, 2014 to 2019, whatever their backlog
272 → 78this company's EBITDA, 2014 to 2015; covenant waiver in 2016
>600k → 150–200kNorwegian harsh-environment rates (USD a day) in three years

Precedents: in the last downturn, backlog did not protect share prices (tiles above). North Atlantic Drilling, a harsh-environment niche stock on which Morgan Stanley initiated coverage in March 2014 with an expected 9.3% yield, suspended its dividend that November. What separated the survivors was contract cover and debt, and on both measures Odfjell is now the best placed in its industry.

Downside markers. With earnings intact and only a de-rating, the share price would fall to about NOK 75 to 85; with one rig idle for half a year and resets 10% lower, to about NOK 50 to 60.

Strongest counter-case. Low leverage, the longest contract cover in the industry and a customer base that booked more work straight after an incident make Odfjell the lowest-risk way to own a driller; in a sector sell-off it could be the refuge.

Against the market. The market treats contract cover as safety. I think earnings to 2027 are safe but the share price is not, because the share price rests on 2029 and on sentiment.

What would change my view. Signed 2029 work for Nordkapp or Aberdeen; a replacement for the spare blowout preventer; a quantified tax rate.

Conclusion: the case is simple and unusually trackable, with low balance-sheet risk, but its risks are lumpy, skewed to the downside and concentrated in 2029, and the share price is more exposed than the earnings.

Score: 55, set by the Rater. The case is as simple as an equity gets (five rigs, days, dayrate, fixed cost, about ten public observations) with leverage falling to about 1.0x on fixed-rate debt, and the memo puts about three chances in four on 2027 EPS within 10% of 1.21; but the range is skewed (one 100-day event is -12%, a clean year +6%), operating events are sudden and uninsured at about one a year, the tax rate is unsettled (EPS 1.17-1.27), and the sector's precedent (-86% in 2014-19, the company's own covenant waiver in 2016) plus a share price that lost NOK 17 on a NOK 3 incident make share-price outcomes far wider than earnings. Between the two Risks groups (38 and 66), below Banca Generali's single sensitivity and level with NKT's visible-but-lumpy execution risk.

#10 Where the stock is in its lifecycle

Evidence: the dashboard's rule says Broadening, but the stock's own signals read later than that. The thesis has stopped adding new sources of upside: the repricing of contracts is done, the Bergen acquisition is done, and deleveraging ends in 2027. Estimate momentum is positive but hollowing (#8), the scope for upgrades is small (#7), the multiple is at the 88th percentile of its five-year range, and the first earnings miss has arrived.

Inference. I place the stock late in the Reinforcing phase: the story is being confirmed, not extended. For the next 12 to 18 months I put about 35% on the Reinforcing phase being prolonged; about 50% on a stall, in which the shares move sideways and pay their dividend while the market absorbs the tax number, the 2029 estimates and the survey budget; and about 15% on a collapse, caused by an oil or sector de-rating, or by a second operating incident alongside a weak Nordkapp rate.

So what. A genuine Broadening phase needs a new source of upside, and the candidates are identifiable: contracts into the 2030s, a capital-returns framework, a sixth rig, or a new leg up in dayrates. None of the four is in the forecasts, and each is observable when it comes.

Strongest counter-case. The dashboard may be right. If the market comes to see Odfjell as a durable income stock, the thesis broadens from "repriced driller" to "income compounder", a phase that lasted five years for Seadrill from 2009.

Against the market. Unanimous Buy ratings imply that the sell-side sees more to come. I see a mature story.

What would change my view. Up: any one of the four new sources of upside appearing. Down: a broker downgrade on valuation.

Conclusion: the stock is late in its Reinforcing phase and more likely to stall than to broaden over the next 12 to 18 months, unless the company supplies a new source of upside.

Score: 46, set by the Rater. The computed Broadening is wrong: no new source has appeared (repricing, the acquisition and deleveraging are done), estimate momentum is hollowing, the first miss has arrived, the multiple is at the 88th percentile of five years and consensus next-year EPS growth is at the 3rd percentile, so this is late Reinforcing with a 50% chance of a stall. That places it just below BP's commodity-peak late Reinforcing and just above Linea Directa.

#11 The fair multiple

The guideline. The dashboard's guideline fair multiple is 13.73 times two-year-forward earnings, the 80th percentile of the stock's ten-year range, set from the Broadening phase. The shares trade on 10.0 times at the model's price (9.2 times in the Phases data of 9 November).

My view: the guideline is about two turns above what the evidence supports as a central case, and is a fair description of the bull case. Four reasons lead to that view.

1
The top of this stock's range was made by trough earnings, not by peak delivery. Every month-end at or above 13.7 times fell in 2016 to 2018, around the turn of 2020 to 2021, or in the first half of 2022, when forward earnings were a fraction of today's. Since mid-2022, through the whole delivery phase, the multiple has ranged from 4.6 to 10.0 times. For a cyclical asset owner, the rule "a multiple higher in the range during peak delivery" runs backwards.
↓
2
Much of the re-rating happens by itself, and that is the useful part. The forward earnings in the multiple fall from about USD 1.15 of EPS today to 1.01 (FY2029) at the model's December 2027 valuation date. If the share price simply holds, the multiple therefore rises from 10.0 to 11.4 times. The guideline thus asks for a share-price gain of about 21%, not 37%. In cash terms, it asks the market to accept an 8.7% yield on a flat dividend that free cash flow only just covers in the survey years, and to pay about 7.2 times 2029 EBITDA.
↓
3
The market's own markers sit below the guideline. The sector trades on about 5.8 times forward EBITDA. The lead broker's target price of NOK 120 equals about 12.8 times our FY2029 EPS. On that broker's net asset value the shares already trade at 1.49 times, above the 1.4 times Seadrill averaged as an income stock. The stock market values the fleet at about USD 700 million a rig, 45% above what Odfjell paid for Bergen eleven months ago.
↓
4
The timing is awkward. The guideline multiple would have to be reached just as the weakest year, 2029, enters the two-year forward window.
➜
Central case: about 11 to 11.5 times FY2029 EPS.

My central case for December 2027 is about 11 to 11.5 times FY2029 EPS, which implies a share price within a few percent of today's and a dividend yield of 10.5% to 11%. The guideline is reachable if two things happen together: Atlantic and at least one 2029 reset are signed for multi-year terms near USD 475,000 to 500,000 a day, and the board states how surplus cash will come back to shareholders. I put that at about one chance in three.

Strongest counter-case. The multiple has risen from 4.6 to 10.0 times in two years as visibility lengthened, so the trend is up. P/E also understates the cash: free cash flow averages USD 1.42 a share over 2027 to 2030, against EPS of about 1.08, because depreciation exceeds through-cycle capital spending by about 100 a year. On cash earnings the guideline value is under 10 times.

Against the market. On our FY2029 EPS the share price is 11.4 times and the brokers' targets are 11.6 to 12.8 times. My central case sits at the share price and just below the targets; the guideline is above every one of them.

What would change my view. Up: the two conditions above. Down: Brent below USD 85, which would pull the range of fair multiples down.

Conclusion: I regard 13.73 times as the bull-case multiple, earned only through contract duration and capital returns, with about 11 to 11.5 times as the central case.

Score: 30, set by the Rater. Neutral on one and dear on the other gives D. The neutral reading flatters: the top of the ten-year range was made on trough earnings, and through the whole delivery phase since mid-2022 the multiple has run 4.6-10.0x with today at the top; some premium to a three-stock cohort is deserved for the best contract cover, and the 10.5% covered yield and the easing to 9.2x hold it off the floor, so it sits in the lower part of the band.

#12 Total shareholder return

What the model shows at the guideline multiple: a large return, all of it from re-rating and dividends.

To 31 December 2027+36.2%+31.1% annualised · NOK 145.78 a share
To 30 June 2029+49.4%+16.4% annualised · NOK 159.83 a share

The multiple and earnings parts multiply rather than add (1.370 times 0.881 is about 1.21), giving a share-price gain of about 21%; dividends come on top of that.

What drives the modelled return.

  • The multiple supplies all of the share-price gain, and more. 13.73 times FY2029 EPS of USD 1.008 is USD 13.84, or NOK 129 a share.
  • Earnings subtract, because the forward year rolls from the 2027 plateau into the 2029 survey year.
  • Dividends are the dependable part: about NOK 16.6 a share by end-2027 and NOK 27.7 by mid-2029, underwritten by contracted cash flow. The dividend is the part of the return that the predictability described in #9 actually supports.
  • The return is front-loaded. The second horizon adds only 13 points over a further 18 months, and all of it is dividends: the share price moves only from NOK 129 to NOK 132. In effect, the model says that after one re-rating Odfjell is a 7% a year stock.

The same forecasts at other multiples (to 31 December 2027).

Each turn of the multiple is worth about 9 points of return, and each USD 0.10 of FY2029 EPS is worth about 12 points at the guideline multiple. On my probability-weighted FY2029 EPS of about 0.91, the guideline return falls from 36% to about 24%.

Inference. The honest statement of the return is the dividend, about 10% a year, plus or minus the change in the multiple. My central case (11 to 11.5 times) gives about +12% to +17% to end-2027 and about 9% to 10% a year to mid-2029. The distribution around the central case is wider below than above until the two conditions in #11 are met.

Strongest counter-case. A 10% cash yield, covered by free cash flow, with leverage of 1.0 times is scarce. If rates of return elsewhere fall, the market may pay for that yield without needing a catalyst.

Against the market. Broker targets imply a share-price gain of 6% on average and 12% at the highest, plus the dividend: above my central case and well short of the guideline return.

What would change my view. A lower share price. At NOK 85, with the forecasts intact, the dividend yield is 13%, and the return from a recovery to today's price alone is 26% before dividends.

Conclusion: the modelled return of +36% to end-2027 is a re-rating to the guideline multiple laid on top of a dependable 15-point dividend stream and falling forward earnings; without the re-rating, the return is the dividend.

Score: 58, set by the Rater. About +16% sits in the C band and maps to about 64; the price gain at the guideline is all re-rating while forward earnings subtract 12 points, the dependable part is the roughly 10% dividend, and the lower tail is fat (NOK 75-85 on a de-rating, NOK 50-60 with an idle rig and lower resets), so I move it down to 58.

#13 Summary conclusion on the business and its investment case

Odfjell Drilling is a first-class operator of five scarce rigs, with the best contract cover and one of the strongest balance sheets in its industry. Its earnings to 2027 are about as predictable as an equity's can be, and its dividend yield of about 10% is well covered until the survey years. That is the strength of the case, and it is real.

It is not the kind of case Richard looks for. The earnings step-up is behind the company, not ahead of it. Outcomes are skewed mildly to the downside, because a full calendar caps the upside and misses arrive in rig-sized steps. Upgrades are unlikely, because there is no guidance to beat and the next sizeable revision, tax, is negative. And the market already agrees with the positive story, at a multiple near the top of its five-year range. What the market has not connected is that the valuation leans on 2029, the year in which contract resets, heavy surveys, the first cash minimum tax and the end of deleveraging coincide.

The constructive reading is that everything that matters here is dated and observable. Four events will tell us most (timeline below). If Atlantic and a 2029 reset are signed for long terms and the board commits to returning surplus cash, the multiple can rise towards the guideline and the modelled return is achievable. If not, Odfjell is a 10% a year income holding with rig-sized risks.

The most attractive way to own the shares is the one the stock has already demonstrated: buy when an operating event or a sector sell-off takes the share price far below the value of an unchanged contract book.

The nearest setup, a Demand-driven EPS Upgrader, needs a demand step-up still ahead in the earnings, and here it is substantively behind the company (forecast EPS plateaus in 2027 and then erodes on flat rates and cost inflation), with no cause for concern clearing and a current operating problem (the 2026 lost days and the Q3 miss) blurring it further; I set aside that the step-up is priced, which topics 7 and 12 judge, so the weak fit rests on the missing element itself.

Topic 9 (55) gives a simple, trackable case with low and falling fixed-rate leverage and contracted 2027 earnings, but the risks are not Richard's paper cuts: they arrive as sudden, uninsured rig-sized steps skewed to the downside, cluster in 2029, and sit on a sector with an 86% drawdown precedent and a share price driven by oil and sentiment at the top of its five-year multiple range, which places it just below Richard's Arteche 60.

How to read this page

Every rating of this stock on one page: the Rater's 1-100 number, its letter and the Rater's own reason (at most three sentences, taken from the ratings file; nothing newly written). The number is the company's approximate standing in the Universe of about 1,300 listed European companies (90 = better than about 9 in 10; 50 = typical). A letter follows its item's rule: rank among the stocks scored (A the top 10%; B+ and B the next 15%; C+, C and C- the next 25%; D the next 25%; F the bottom 25%); or Richard's cut-offs on the measure for the four numerical topics (forecast financials, current momentum, the fair multiple, total shareholder return). On the change-forces items the number carries a sign (50 = neither positive nor negative) and the letter is the rank, so read the two together. "9th of 30 stocks scored" is the stock's place on that item. A dashed badge is provisional (fewer than 30 stocks scored).
